analysis.title: The One Price To Watch In The Bonfire Of Data Centers
key_insights: GPU rental prices are the indicator for whether the post-midterm data-center backlash threatens the AI trade. They show whether compute supply is falling relative to demand.

Many midterm elections worked as referendums on AI, with some of the largest swings to Democrats in states with the biggest data-center footprint. How hard Democrats will clamp down on projects is still unknown.
GPU rental prices show no change in their upward trend since the elections. If fewer data centers are built or greenlit, or more are delayed, rental prices are likely to rise more steeply.

Scarcer compute favors hyperscalers, who own or lease up to three-quarters of existing US AI data-center capacity. It hurts those effectively short compute (AI labs and neoclouds) and those who build, kit out and power data centers (Nvidia, Eaton, Vertiv).
Since the elections, hyperscaler stocks have bounced while neocloud, power-provider and semiconductor stocks are all lower.

Modo Energy estimates 40% of announced data centers could be disrupted by moratoriums, affecting up to 256 GW. It still sees 2035 capacity falling only about 4 GW against over 600 GW planned, because delayed projects proceed and others move to friendlier US states or abroad.

Back-of-envelope offset: Epoch AI puts capex at $37B per gigawatt ($18.5B a year over two years). CoreWeave rents capacity at about $40B annualized per gigawatt, so a 30% rental rise adds $12B a year. That means 1.5 GW of existing compute repricing 30% covers the lost capex revenue from 1 GW of new build.
Most compute is pre-contracted. If 10%-20% of the installed ~30 GW of US compute can reprice quickly, economics shift from building new capacity to monetizing installed capacity.

The thesis is flawed if capex and GPU rental prices start to fall at the same time. Otherwise the worst case is a rotation within the AI trade, and the market may even absorb Anthropic and OpenAI pulling IPOs because part of the economics accrues to hyperscalers.
Data-center moratoria also let firms cancel projects without conceding that there is already too much compute.

Near-term stabilization case: hedge funds, the main drivers of last week's decline, have cut gross positions almost 9 points and beta-adjusted positions nearly 16 points (Goldman Sachs data). Morgan Stanley sees net hedge fund risk at a one-year low.

Retail has not joined the selling in a substantial way based on leveraged ETF flows. Institutions are slower to act and still hold large tech positions, so neither is likely to pull out absent a clear sign the AI trade is over.

The author's Recession Gauge shows little sign of a downturn, and deep stock declines (over 20%) are rare outside recessions. A mass nationwide cancellation of data centers would badly hurt the economy but is not the base case.

sector_views.rationale: They own or lease up to three-quarters of existing US AI data-center capacity, so tighter compute supply and higher rental prices favor them. They have bounced since the elections.

sector_views.sector: Neoclouds, AI labs, data-center builders and power equipment
sector_views.rationale: They depend on continued new build-out or have an acute need for compute, so a data-center clampdown makes conditions tougher. Neocloud, power-provider and semiconductor stocks are lower since the elections.

risk_factors: Capex is heavily rolled back as fewer data centers are built.
Short-term bottlenecks could lift GPU rental prices regardless of Modo's long-term capacity estimates.
Capex and GPU rental prices falling at the same time would show the compute-repricing thesis is flawed.
Further near-term turbulence, with vol-control funds still needing to cut risk and a spy scandal at the world's second-largest firm.
Anthropic and OpenAI could pull IPOs if they cannot secure enough compute.
Hedge funds are highly leveraged and concentrated in the same stocks, so another mini-meltdown is possible.
A mass nationwide cancellation of data centers would be a severe blow to the economy.
Reasons other than a data-center backlash could cause the AI trade to implode.
charts_described: Modo Energy chart shows a net fall of only about 4 GW in capacity in 2035 versus over 600 GW planned, with the expected Texas (ERCOT) shortfall mostly made up elsewhere.
vol_and_positioning: Goldman Sachs data shows hedge fund gross positions down almost 9 percentage points and beta-adjusted positions down nearly 16 percentage points over the last week.
Morgan Stanley sees net hedge fund risk at a one-year low.
Vol-control funds still need to reduce risk to reflect higher volatility.
Leveraged ETF flows show retail has not joined the selling in a substantial way.
Institutional ownership in tech remains high.
geopolitical: US midterm elections turned partly into referendums on AI, with large swings to Democrats where data centers have the biggest footprint, raising the risk of data-center moratoriums.
A spy scandal at the world's second-largest firm is described as brewing, adding to market unease after last Thursday's sharp decline.

tension_points.bull_case: Higher GPU rental prices on installed capacity can offset lost new-build capex revenue. A 30% rental rise on 1.5 GW covers one gigawatt of lost capex, and many blocked projects move to friendlier jurisdictions, so Modo sees only a 4 GW net shortfall in 2035.
tension_points.bear_case: Modo estimates 40% of announced data centers, up to 256 GW, could be disrupted. Capex could be heavily rolled back, most compute is pre-contracted so repricing is limited, and neoclouds, AI labs and equipment makers are hurt.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Capex and GPU rental prices start to fall at the same time.

tension_points.theme: near-term stock stabilization after AI selloff
tension_points.bull_case: Hedge funds have de-risked sharply, retail has not joined the selling, institutions move slowly and hold large tech positions, and the Recession Gauge shows little sign of a downturn.
tension_points.bear_case: Vol-control funds still need to reduce risk, a spy scandal is brewing at the world's second-largest firm, and leveraged hedge funds can trigger another mini-meltdown.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A clear indication that the AI trade is over would prompt retail and institutional investors to sell.

theme_stances.key_argument: A data-center clampdown most likely rotates the AI trade toward hyperscalers rather than ending it, because higher compute prices can offset lost capex.
theme_stances.evidence: the worst we may see is a rotation in the AI trade

theme_stances.key_argument: Hedge funds drove the decline and have already cut risk, while retail and institutions are less likely to sell without a clear sign the AI trade is over.
theme_stances.evidence: hedge funds, the primary drivers of last week’s decline, have de-risked non-trivially
